You will learn why speed matters so much, what a posted limit really means, why some roads also post a minimum, when you must slow below the limit, and how work zones change the rules. The goal is not simply to stay under a number, but to choose a speed that fits the road, the weather and the people around you.","fact_ids":["sec08-F03","sec08-F04","sec08-F05","sec08-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Speed decides severity","fact_ids":["sec08-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Biggest factor in crash severity.","fact_ids":["sec08-F03"]},{"text":"Many deadly crashes involve speeding.","fact_ids":["sec08-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Speed is the biggest factor in how severe a crash is, and many deadly Colorado highway crashes involve drivers going too fast. The faster you go, the more distance you cover before you can react, the longer it takes to stop, and the more force there is in a collision. A small increase in speed can turn a minor bump into a serious injury. That is why so many rules in this chapter come back to slowing down: around curves, in neighborhoods, in work zones and in poor weather. Practice questions may describe a nervous driver crawling on a freeway in good weather and ask whether that is acceptable. It is not. During the first two, the car is still traveling at full speed. So a distracted driver, who takes longer to recognize the hazard, adds distance before braking even begins. And at higher speeds, every part grows.
